The New York Tribune, of the 9th inst, in
speaking ofletters it has received from Washing
ton, says:


''One of them mentions that Mr.. Packenham,
British Minster) has privately expressed bis be-
lief that the Oregon question will be settled with
out war, unless there shall be a serious effort 10
make trouble about it in Congress-, or by the
press"


That, we take it, is sufficiently cool Not
content with calumnies of all sorts, heaped upon
us through the English press; nor with the efforts
of such British presses in this country, as the
Albion; nor yet with aid SO literally bestowed by
the American press, in the form OF advocacy oI
the "yelding policy"-not content, we say, with
all this, we must now be threatened with war by
the British Minister, at Washington, if we pre-
sumo either in Congress, or through the press,
TO maintain them!


This device, so peculiarly British, seems to
cover two intentions; first, by threatening US with
war, if we attempt to snake trouble' about Ore
gon, the hope evidently is that more or less oi
the "yielding policy" presses will endeavor to
keep down the rising feeling of the nation upon
the subject of our Oregon rights: and second
when the war does come, as the English say il
shall, if we do not "yeld,' then they can say, as
the British government ever did say, "our oppo-
nents have forced us into war, against our ev.
Iery effort to prevent it."


The fatering epithet, mob, is constantly ap
piled TO the people of this country, by the Eng
lish writer's and editors; and they wish the press
not to move this "mob" to assert the rights oi
the nation. This term, by the way, is favorite
one with the English translator Of Thiers' His
tory of the French Revoution--his copy being
the only one known in this country Whenever
the author speaks of the people, as he needs must

passed which despoiled you, fellow-citizens
of Howard, of your just rights, and which
violated the principle of republicanism. For these reasons

with direct view to suppress the voice of
the west in the State? This is not denied,

made boast that no west should go to

party are opposed to equal representation;

notions of Justice and Law in community of
equal freedom, when his opinion of the fitness of
a fellow citizen for high judicial trust depends
upon the question "to what political party does he
belong?"

Suppose again we were to see the Court pro-
ceeding at another time to make nominations for
the same office, and uniformly to reject every

the men upon whom the STATE DEPEND for its support and defence in every possible event and who are therefore precisely entitled TO be spared from undue share of public misfortune. In the higher grades of education thus want is far less seriously felt. The number of pupils in the university, colleges, academies, classical and grammar schools of this State being some less two per cent of our whole population, nevertheless than it is to be found in any of the States except those of New England, and less so there only by an algebraic difference which is unquestionably owing to the facility and cheapness with which education may be had in the midst of country village population much more crowded than ours. Evidence of this is shown by the fact that the eleven thousand and eighty three students which belong to the grammar schools and academies of this State, distributed amongst three hundred and eighty two schools being an average of twenty nine to the school, whilst the 22,000 students of like kind in New England, parcelled out amongst six hundred and thirty schools, in the proper proportion, separately, of ninety seven to each school in Maine, 85 in New Hampshire, &c. in Massachusetts, and upwards as many in New England generally. Thus more men are taught in less schools, the number of schools and consequently the number of pupils per school being much greater in each particular one. In other words we have an almost equal number of our young men taught at our colleges as are taught in our common schools. This shows that the number of scholars taught in our State is much less than in New England.

Realizing now the importance and cruelty guilty in such a neglect, and the want of our people, we must not any longer only consider the 16,600 in this STATE, who are of suitable age, that between 15 and 20, 16,600 only are receiving any kind of education; and if the 10,000 towards of those who are credited to the colleges, academies and classical schools be deducted, there may be left but 6,600 who are going to common schools and 1,000 who appear to be going to school whatsoever.

Such state affairs in the midst of civilization like ours, and showing all the faults of liberty and government like ours, absolutely appalls and calls for redress with power of authority, in which words can do nothing. Let the fostering hand of the State be extended for this redress, and extended in chief to those who are most dependent and in want. In our case the task and controlling duty, the facts presented demonstrate, is not to provide for the highest grades of scholarship so much as its humblest elements; remodel the system of common education such that it offers the alphabet of knowledge to all who will receive it, and can rescue at once from the destiny of uneducated ignorance the helpless and thousands of youth upon whom nothing is done; it will be helped beyond being declined and evaded any longer, and the entire body of our people will be saved. All defend, all and GOVERN, and should be expected to do so. This is a wrong and injury ALREADY done, and our labors are hereafter to pay for it. The neglect has done much harm in this State, and our money and energy should be lost before this work of justice is done.

I have submitted in former messages what seemed a suitable plan for the reconnaissance of this work and respectfully refer to it now, in hopes that it has been successfully matured and supplied. That plan generally is to establish in each COUNTY, with the consent of majority of taxpayers, free schools for education, for the support of these schools from the quotas of the present school tax, and such additional sum as may be found necessary to be made, and united in given proportions to the schools wherever by vote and local account, and managed under county tribunals and these in turn under the general supervision of central and controlling authorities. Each county to undertake this plan and, having adopted it, should be able to do so, and in all cases the plan is accepted, rejected, or renounced, to control the school quota each county must, just as at present.

Without illustrating the plan by additional detail, it is perhaps safe to say that by placing the adoption in the county upon the express consent of its own taxpayers, you appeal to those who are the most concerned in its interests and most with the weight of income and business to decide whether it will suit them or not; you enable each county in its adoption, modify and mature it according to its judgment and its own circumstances and wants; you connect the local support by surrounding taxpayers to support these SCHOOLS.

We may have helped many thousands in our people who are the backbone and the main force of society, and assist them to rise from the humbler agencies for education to those of higher and more expensive kind. Should I omit part of my duty to the public, I did not recommend to you the power of making an early and thorough enquiry into the management and wants of the Universities of the State. This institution is a noble monument to the wisdom of its founders and to the patriotism of the authorities. It does upon the resources of the State what all should do: be prudent in nothing which is necessary to render it an instrument of usefulness to the county, and whether it be of more or less expense than it is of benefit in other respects, it is a work which may well be said to your local investigation and your duty commend in this State.

I submit to your legislation, and you may go to the realization of its usefulness.

Thus began the scientific life of M Arago-a life

What characterized Nj. Arago was the diversity

of Europe professor and learned man, he
brought into the oratorical jouss an abundant, lu-

ity had even something dazzling in Nj. Arago, and
made him ono Of the most fertile plain-dealers that
has ever appeared.


A man thus organized could so much the less re-
sign himself to live apart from politics, he was
also called to them by naturally ruling spirit and
an Immense need OF activity; for erything seemed
equally to suit this richly endowed nature--retre-
ment and action, the tranquility Of study and the
hustle of human affairs, the solitary contemplation of
worlds and the forum filed with storms


Powerful from science, NJ Arago was perhaps
still morse so from passion. He was not able long
to content himself with the kind of dictatorship
which the academy of sciences had voluntarily con-
hded TO him, though there were there obstacles TO
vanquish struggles to sustain, and enemies to
whelm. But that M. ARGOS abilities might find

combats were necessary. He therefore rushed to-
wards political regions; and with thatforc of attrac-
ton which it exercises all sovereign natures,
democracy irreslstbly attracted him. And who
more than he, was made to figure there with ecat
No less capable of moving, than of instructing the
people, he awed someby the authority Of his name
he won others by the energy of his spirit warm
hearted moreover and without gall.


AT need, the part of tribune would not have
been above his ardor. And yet he had not that Kind

TO be intoxicated with contradiction, and TO be borne

toned, as professor, TO applause, Nj. Arago only

evening" walking in the garden Of the observatory,
with some members of his family and friend, he
was pleased TO state the thoughts of which dis
course that he was TO pronounce in the Chamber Of
Deputies next day, consisted. The question wac,

tracing the history of the services rendered by them

from their bosom Carried away by the ardor of
an improvisation, which at first familiar, eradu-
ally he became animated exalted--at last sublime.
We seem to him still on that elevated terrace,
which overooks Paris, with his tall figure, like that

tended, his hair agtated by the wind his eye full of

The next day we went to hear M. Arngo IN the

that recognised him, attentive did he appear

M. Aragos eminent qualities were, nevertheless,
not unaoyed. To have Interchangeable and sole
end in view to know how TO concentrate ones ac-
tvity, to manage prudenty ones alliances and re-
sources, to dependents for ones sefby
tnued system of thoughtful attentions and patient
consideration, to avoid all enemies but such 1t is
useful to havethis it is that behooves the head of
party, in society which balanced by the love OF
change and thesfear of crises. Now, M. Arago had
less perseverance than impeuosty; he allowed htm-
self to be too easily distracted from one great design
by secondary prescriptions; he lesScned himself
by expanding the force Of his will over too many
objects time; he only half knew te art of discp-
lining resistance under him; intrepid and faithful in
his friendships he did not sufficiently conclia,e the
Indifferent and his impetuous personality more than
once wounded an extremely suspicious party. To
say all in word he sacrificed more to the passion
Of the moment than to his great aim. Obstinacy
and calculation in passion composed the whole ge-
MUS of Ppm. With such genius as that, you
may prepare revolutions-M. Arago had the genius
| which determines them.


However that may be, M. Arago at the time of
which we speak, made no mystery of his hopes,
and the democratic party might already salute him

Spain; and in the accomplishment of the mission he
endured thousand sufferings, faced thousand dan-
gers. He passed SIX months on the isolated peak of
mountains, awaiting the hour when observation
would be possible. At the time of the first entry of
the French into the peninsula, he was, as envoy of
Napoleon, plunged into the prison of Valencia; after
wards taken to Algiers, he returning to France,
when captured within sight of Marseilles by Span-
ish corsair, he was brought back to Rose, then
thrown on board prison-ship at Palamos. During
his captivity at Rose and Palamos, he carried his
devotion to science far too refuse to escape, that
he might not lose his observations and instruments.
Thus began the scientific life of M. Arago—a life
marked by crowd of celebrated labors and admirable
discoveries.


What characterized M. Arago was the diversity
of his aptitudes. Renowned throughout the whole
of Europe professor and learned man, he
brought into the oratorical joust an abundant, lu-
minous eloquence, teeming with facts, quotations,
surprising details; and certainly among the great
writers of his age none could have flattered himself
to exceed him in the copiousness, the versatility and
above all, the clearness of his style. This last qual-
ity had even something dazzling in M. Arago, and
made him one of the most fertile plain-dealers that
has ever appeared.


A man thus organized could so much the less re-
sign himself to live apart from politics, he was
also called to them by naturally ruling spirit and
an immense need of activity; for everything seemed
equally to suit this richly endowed nature—retre-
atment and action, the tranquility of study and the
hustle of human affairs, the solitary contemplation of
worlds and the forum filled with storms.


Powerful from science, M. Arago was perhaps
still more so from passion. He was not able long
to content himself with the kind of dictatorship
which the academy of sciences had voluntarily con-
ferred to him, though there were obstacles to
vanquish, struggles to sustain, and enemies to
whelm. But that M. Arago's abilities might find
sufficient employment, other obstacles and other
combats were necessary. He therefore rushed to-
wards political regions; and with that force of attrac-
tion which it exercises all sovereign natures,
democracy irresistibly attracted him. And who
more than he, was made to figure there with éclat.
No less capable of moving, than of instructing the
people, he awed some by the authority of his name,
he won others by the energy of his spirit, warm-
hearted moreover and without gall.


At need, the part of tribune would not have
been above his ardor. And yet he had not that kind
of superiority which enabled Mirabeau to sport with
storms, to breathe amid them with proud facility,
to be intoxicated with contradiction, and to be borne
on the very anastomoses reused about him. Ac-
customed, as professor, to applause, M. Arago only
displayed himself entirely before audience dispo-
sed to comprehend and like him. The antipathy of
hostile assembly, without overcoming his courage,
impaired his sources of inspiration. One spring
evening walking in the garden of the observatory,
with some members of his family and friends, he
was pleased to state the thoughts of which his dis-
course that he was to pronounce in the Chamber of
Deputies next day, consisted. The question was,
to revenge the people for patrician contempt, by
tracing the history of the services rendered by them
to science, and counting up the great men sprung
from their bosom. Carried away by the ardor of
an improvisation, which at first familiar, gradu-
ally he became animated exalted—at last sublime.
We seem to him still on that elevated terrace,
which overlooks Paris, with his tall figure, like that
of an Arab chief, his head uncovered, his arm ex-
tended, his hair agitated by the wind, his eye full of
fire, the upper part of his forehead lightened by the
rays of the sun, which was descending the horizon
in golden vapor. No; never had man more
majestic aspect, and never did thoughts proceeding
from the heart assume more solemn or noble forms.
The next day we went to hear M. Arago in the
Chamber of Deputies, and it was with difficulty
that we recognised him, attentive did he appear
to the wretched murmurs which the eulogium of
the people drew from the assembly!


M. Arago's eminent qualities were, nevertheless,
not unalloyed. To have interchangeable and sole
end in view to know how to concentrate one's ac-
tivity, to manage prudently one's alliances and re-
sources, to depend for one's self on a
tuned system of thoughtful attentions and patient
consideration, to avoid all enemies but such as it is
useful to have—this it is that behooves the head of
party, in society which is balanced by the love of
change and the fear of crises. Now, M. Arago had
less perseverance than impetuosity; he allowed him-
self to be too easily distracted from one great design
by secondary prescriptions; he lessened himself
by expanding the force of his will over too many
objects at a time; he only half knew the art of discip-
lining resistance under him; intrepid and faithful in
his friendships he did not sufficiently conciliate the
indifferent and his impetuous personality more than
once wounded an extremely suspicious party. To
say all in a word he sacrificed more to the passion
of the moment than to his great aim. Obstinacy
and calculation in passion composed the whole ge-
nus of him. With such genius as that, you
may prepare revolutions—M. Arago had the genius
which determines them.


However that may be, M. Arago at the time of
which we speak, made no mystery of his hopes,
and the democratic party might already salute him
as one of its heads.

And when the falsehood is detected, it is most natural to infer guilt, which the falsehood was intended to conceal.


But Cunningham not guilty of the murder, yet he told a lie. His unbalanced mind oscillated and finally settled to a falsehood and he inflicted upon himself the double terrors of detection of the lie, and the almost consequent presumption of murder. The lie was easily proved upon him, and, consequently, the homicide is naturally inferred.


What is valuable in the teachings of this trial, for all trials teachings is the enforcement of the importance of truth at all times and especially on circumstances, where there is presumption suspicion of crime, for the lie, hastily formed and uttered, cannot (and it ought to be considerably) stand the close scrutiny to which the crime will render it liable; and it will, therefore, rather to expose than to hide the guilt. The blanket that is drawn up to conceal the face, will probably leave bare the feet, and the exposure of either extremity will afford evidence of personal presence.


Had Cunningham promptly and candidly explained to the Coroner or others, who first saw the body of the drowned person, all that he confessed to the Judge and Jury, he would probably have been considered a candid man. He yielded to his fears, and his distrust, and told a lie. He had, of course, never been taught the whole importance of truth. He had not practiced against adverse temptations the utterance OF truth. His impulses were strong; his fears were greater than his principles, and he fell. Few, indeed, suffer much from a lie that was not intended for their neighbours' hurt, but none can tell what will be the result of the attempt at false concealment and none may rightly complain of what may be regarded as severe punishment when that punishment is seen to be a natural and inevitable consequence of the fault.


Parents will probably see, in the circumstance of Cunningham, a lesson in apprehensions for the fate of those providentially entrusted to their care and they will apply a lesson to the young, far more effective than any we can give, and at which we only hint in these remarks, which we conclude by copying the following opposite lines:


"Face thine enemies-accusers,
Soon the prison, rack or rod!
And if thou hast TRUTH to utter,
Speak and leave the rest to God"

THE BRITISH PRESS IN AMERICA.—In our last, we called attention to the British principles and feelings of the National Intelligencer. We did so to give warning, so far as our feeble voice would go, to the people, of the dangerous influence at work, in our very midst, to undermine and sap the foundations of our Republican institutions—an influence the more dangerous, because exerted under the insidious guise of friendship, while they are seemingly alive with the rankest anti-American sentiments, and indissolubly bound to promote British interests. We say British interests, because the influences we deprecate as inimical to our own country, whether directed in favor of one foreign nation or another, ever tend to the benefit of Great Britain, as she is the only hereditary and implacable rival and enemy of the United States, the only foreign nation to derive advantage or qualification from our injury. It behooves us, then, as people, jealous of our rights, proud of our institutions, and grateful for the great legacy of independence bequeathed us by our fathers, to scrutinize well the conduct, the feelings, and the policies of those who zeal, to give direction to public sentiment—who assume the sanction of giving form and pressure to the popular will. In confirmation of our own opinions, and to show that we are not alone in the views we have presented, we copy the following from the New Orleans Picayune of June 13—a paper, respectful in its political position, yet edited by Americans. It does not mention the Intelligencer by name; yet the indication cannot be mistaken.

"It would, indeed, surprise us if an Englishman and journalist did not contend earnestly for the supremacy and rights, real or imaginary, of his own country; but deletions of this sort in the American press occur frequently and serve to excite no special wonder. We do know journals that are recognized leaders in political circles that have never yet, since we were old enough to regard such things, take the part of the American government in any quarrel it has had with foreign ones—journals that made it their business to assail our government in its controversy with France, in its troubles with England, in its difficulties with Mexico, on the right-of-search question, on boundaries, and even condemned the chastisements that were inflicted upon barbarous and cannibal islanders, who massacred our merchant sails in distant seas. These are melancholy truths. It is not possible that the United States can always be in the wrong; but, according to those journalists, we are never right—our real rights are treated by them as imaginary, and imaginary ones are scolded at. We are not objecting to legitimate differences of opinion in respect to the acquisition of territory, or the conduct of our foreign relations; we allude to those quarrels—such as seems likely to arise in regard to Oregon—such as took place in the Esser affair—such as threatened war in regard to the navigation of the African seas—such as the chastisement of the cannibals of Qualah Bato—such as the coercion of the French Legation—such as arise out of the seizure and liberation of our slaves by the inhabitants of Nassau and other British West India dependencies such as spring up in the exercise of the right of search—such as threaten us in the triple conspiracy of England, Mexico, and France (as is now supposed) touching annexation—such, in fact, as arise out of any possible aggression of England, and conceivable assumption of Europe, or any imaginable conduct of Christian, Pagan, civilized, or savage nations. We are persuaded that the Whig has sympathized with our mortification, many times, in noticing the deflections of which we speak; and more especially must our friends lament with us that so many of our contemporaries never saw the slightest objection to the allusion in Mr. Folks' inaugural to the Oregon question, all this dust is raised about, that they got the cue from the British press."
